lessons.when: a supplier counters above a buyer proposal but continues to reduce its price
lessons.action: consider holding a credible proposal for another round rather than improving it automatically
lessons.why: a further supplier concession may make the existing proposal acceptable without the buyer giving up more value
lessons.evidence: After another supplier e-mail saying “Our counter-offer,” the buyer repeated its package options unchanged; the supplier replied, “We agree.”

lessons.when: offering the supplier a choice among packages with the same quality commitment but different prices and complaint remedies
lessons.action: check that the added remedy is worth its price premium to the buyer before inviting the supplier to choose
lessons.why: the supplier can select the higher-priced package; giving it the choice does not ensure the buyer captures the greatest saving
lessons.evidence: The buyer wrote, “We can offer either of these packages - please choose the one that suits you better,” and the supplier accepted the package with the higher price and a complaint chargeback rather than the lower-priced package with the same quality commitment.

lessons.when: the supplier proposes a price increase despite a contractual notice requirement or a favorable demand forecast
lessons.action: cite the relevant contract and forecast records, and ask the supplier to reflect both in a revised offer
lessons.why: The supplier checked these facts, acknowledged them, and used the forecast to revise its calculation.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “We also checked the notice period data you cited; it holds and we took it into account. We did not know that - a fair point. We have also taken your positive volume forecast into account, which allows us to adjust our calculation.”

lessons.when: the supplier justifies an increase using cost indices
lessons.action: weight each index movement by its stated share of costs before countering the proposed increase
lessons.why: The weighted impact provides a case-specific basis for challenging an increase that exceeds the cited cost pressure.
lessons.evidence: Buyer: “Weighted with the cost structure of this part, the index movements explain about +2.3% on the price - not 9.5%.”

lessons.when: the supplier counters above a buyer-proposed price while adopting the buyer's proposed timing
lessons.action: do not treat agreement on timing as full acceptance of the package; evaluate the remaining price gap before accepting
lessons.why: A supplier can build on one option without accepting all its terms. Here the deal closed after that counter, while the result captured only part of the possible saving.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “Building on your third option, we propose a revised price of EUR 136.30 per unit for this later effective date.” Result: “score 0.56.”

lessons.evidence: “represents our absolute limit” and “In response to your movement, we are prepared to make a further concession”

lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “We can accept your terms and await your order.” The next supplier e-mail says: “Thank you for your order. Our order confirmation is attached.”

lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “if you can't show me the competition's prices, I can't just drop mine.”

lessons.when: a supplier calls a revised offer final
lessons.action: Treat the claim as a decision point, not proof that no further concession is possible; weigh one more credible request against the risk of losing the offer.
lessons.why: In this session, the final-offer message followed several concessions, but the back-office notes also show that the supplier had previously considered walking away. Neither possibility should be ignored.
lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “This is our final offer (letztes Angebot). Please decide.” Back-office note: “My call: walk_away.”

lessons.action: Hold the buyer's proposal rather than improving it again without a reciprocal move.
lessons.why: An unchanged supplier offer gives no evidence that another buyer concession is needed; holding preserves the remaining saving while leaving room for the supplier to propose an alternative.

lessons.evidence: Supplier: “faster payment terms do allow us to adjust the price.”

lessons.when: the supplier accepts a cited delivery-performance concern but says it does not affect its calculation
lessons.action: Pursue a delivery remedy separately instead of relying on the same concern to win a price reduction.
lessons.why: The supplier may verify an operational problem yet keep it outside its price decision.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “We checked the delivery record data you cited; it holds, but it does not change our calculation.”

lessons.when: the supplier cites a price freeze but invites discussion of other terms
lessons.action: Seek explicit prices for alternative packages of commitment and payment terms rather than treating the stated freeze as the end of negotiation.
lessons.why: A supplier that will not grant a standalone price cut may still price a package differently when another term changes.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “Our management has frozen all price reductions … We can talk about the terms instead - payment, volume or contract length.”

lessons.action: State a defensible commitment limited to the volume actually available to that supplier, then request a revised price before accepting its current offer.

lessons.when: a supplier attributes a price difference to stock allocation or service levels
lessons.action: Specify which services the buyer needs and ask for a separately priced, reduced-service alternative before treating the item as a simple stock purchase.
lessons.why: The supplier says those commitments carry costs. A clearly reduced scope gives it a reason to change its quote while making the quality trade-off visible.
lessons.evidence: “The difference between list and renewal quotes accounts for dedicated stock allocations and specific service levels.”

lessons.when: the buyer has improved its proposed packages but the supplier repeats its offer unchanged
lessons.action: Do not improve the buyer’s terms again without a specific reciprocal concession; instead, test a new source of value or compare the standing offer with the alternative.
lessons.why: In this exchange, raising the proposed prices did not produce a supplier price step. Further unilateral movement would give away value without evidence that it changes the supplier’s decision.
lessons.evidence: Buyer: “We have raised our proposed prices at a real cost to us and expect a step from you in return.” Supplier: “We have reviewed your revised options, but we must hold our offer.”

lessons.when: a supplier justifies its price with rising cost indices and the buyer’s cited index data also show an increase
lessons.action: Calculate the weighted effect of the cited cost movements and challenge any unsupported difference, rather than relying on the same rising index as an argument for a lower price.
lessons.why: The supplier treated the buyer’s data as confirmation of its cost argument. The strength of a price challenge depends on what the movements imply for total cost, not on citing the indices alone.
lessons.evidence: “Your figures confirm our case: that driver rose. That does not change our position.”

lessons.when: the supplier quotes different prices for different payment terms
lessons.action: Compare the complete packages before choosing; make any move toward faster payment conditional on an adequate price reduction.
lessons.why: The supplier prices payment timing into its offer, so a lower unit price can come at the cost of less favourable payment terms.
lessons.evidence: “As an alternative, in response to your movement, we are prepared to offer a unit price … based on your proposed … payment terms.”

lessons.when: the supplier has made little movement and the buyer's last offer remains far away
lessons.action: Do not simply repeat the same options and expect another concession; introduce a credible new trade or decide against the available offer.
lessons.why: In this session, an unchanged buyer offer led the supplier to hold its position and declare it final.
lessons.evidence: Buyer: “We keep our offer as it stands.” Supplier: “You have maintained your previous offer without further movement.” Back office: “My call: hold.”

lessons.when: the supplier justifies its quote with cost pressures and the buyer has a credible cost estimate
lessons.action: present the estimate and ask the supplier to check it, then use the response to support a revised offer
lessons.why: a verified estimate gives the buyer's price request a factual basis, though it may not overcome the supplier's other constraints by itself
lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “We checked the should cost data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

lessons.when: the supplier says a price freeze limits reductions but identifies terms it can trade
lessons.action: test packages that change the terms the supplier values, rather than relying on a price request alone
lessons.why: the supplier may be able to justify a concession through a valuable commitment even when it says base-price reductions are frozen
lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “We can talk about the terms instead - payment, volume or contract length.”

lessons.when: the supplier says an existing commitment is insufficient and asks whether another commitment is feasible
lessons.action: answer the feasibility question directly; offer a binding change only if it is workable, or ask what concession the supplier would exchange for it
lessons.why: repeating the same package leaves the supplier's stated condition unmet and can cause it to hold its offer
lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “our request for a higher volume commitment has not been addressed”; back-office note: “My call: hold.”

lessons.when: a lower price is offered alongside less favourable non-price terms
lessons.action: compare the complete packages before choosing or countering
lessons.why: a nominal price reduction can give back value through payment terms or other conditions
lessons.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “the extended contract term enables us to offer a revised price”; a later e-mail says “a longer contract term alone” cannot support further reductions and instead proposes changing payment terms.

lessons.when: a verified competing quote is materially lower than a supplier’s offer
lessons.action: cite the competing quote and ask the supplier to improve its offer
lessons.why: the supplier may treat credible competition as a reason to concede rather than dismissing the comparison
lessons.evidence: “We checked the rival quote data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

lessons.when: a supplier makes a first concession after seeing a much lower rival quote
lessons.action: treat the concession as a possible first step, not necessarily its limit, and ask for another improvement before committing
lessons.why: the back-office notes show a deliberate partial concession while the supplier assessed further movement
lessons.evidence: “The buyer shows a much lower rival quote. I give half the step now and check the rest.”

lessons.when: a supplier says it still needs to review its price internally
lessons.action: do not place the order before following up on that review
lessons.why: accepting immediately closes the negotiation while a further price decision may still be pending
lessons.evidence: “We need to clarify this internally - we will come back to you on price.” The next supplier message was: “Thank you for your order. Our order confirmation is attached.”

lessons.when: comparing offers with different delivery and payment terms
lessons.action: compare complete packages and test the cost of changing terms before treating an opening price as the cheaper alternative
lessons.why: a supplier may reprice the offer when requested terms alter its costs; a shorter lead time can require overtime
lessons.evidence: “Your requested terms change our costs; our Angebot for them follows.” “A shorter Lieferzeit means overtime; that is priced in.”

lessons.when: a documented demand forecast supports a larger purchase
lessons.action: cite the verifiable change when requesting a lower price, but distinguish a forecast from a binding volume commitment
lessons.why: the supplier checked the forecast and considered it, while indicating that a firm volume commitment could justify a further reduction
lessons.evidence: “We checked the volume change data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.” “A binding higher volume would help us and can improve the price.”

lessons.when: the supplier offers the same price for a longer commitment
lessons.action: do not extend the agreement solely for a promised price benefit; ask for a distinct price step or keep the shorter commitment
lessons.why: planning security benefits the supplier, but an unchanged price gives the buyer no saving in exchange for the added commitment
lessons.evidence: “Your latest offer keeps the same unit price for the longer term, so we would still need a price step for that commitment.”

lessons.when: both sides are still moving on price
lessons.action: make a measured concession conditional on a reciprocal step, rather than immediately accepting the supplier’s counteroffer
lessons.why: the supplier explicitly treated the buyer’s movement as a reason to move again
lessons.evidence: “We appreciate your concession and are pleased to take a step toward you in return.”

lessons.when: the supplier repeats its position and labels it final
lessons.action: compare the complete offer with the available alternative; accept if it is worthwhile, rather than assuming another unchanged request will yield a concession
lessons.why: the back-office decision was to hold, not counter, at that stage
lessons.evidence: “My call: hold.” “We answer with our final offer.”

lessons.when: the supplier justifies its price with cost indices and cost weights
lessons.action: Calculate the weighted effect and challenge any gap between that effect and the proposed increase.
lessons.why: A specific calculation gives the supplier a reason to reconsider its opening price, even if it will not disclose its full cost breakdown.
lessons.evidence: Buyer: “the weighted effect on the price is about +7.5%, not the 11.01% you ask for.” Supplier: “we have carefully considered your calculations” and then lowered its offer.

lessons.when: two buyer packages give the supplier the same non-price terms
lessons.action: Do not offer a higher price in one package without receiving a distinct benefit in return.
lessons.why: The supplier can use the higher-priced package as the basis for its counteroffer, weakening the lower-priced request.
lessons.evidence: Buyer: “Option A is the leaner fixed-price route.” The two fixed-price packages had the same other terms. Supplier: “Building on your Option B” when countering from the higher-priced package.

lessons.when: the supplier values a dependable sales horizon
lessons.action: Test whether a longer agreement earns a meaningful price concession before committing to it.
lessons.why: Planning stability can make a package acceptable to the supplier, but the buyer should capture part of that value.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “We appreciate your offer of a ... agreement, which provides valuable planning stability for both of us.” Its back office then recorded: “we agree.”

lessons.when: a supplier offers a lower headline price with an index adjustment than without one
lessons.action: Compare the full indexed and fixed-price packages, including future adjustment risk, rather than treating the headline reduction as pure savings.
lessons.why: An index clause shifts some future cost risk back to the buyer; the deal’s value depends on more than its initial unit price.
lessons.evidence: Supplier: “Our primary proposal” included a “Preisgleitklausel”; it also offered an alternative “with no Preisgleitklausel.” The final deal retained the index clause, and the result identified index risk among the costs left in the deal.

lessons.when: a supplier's proposed quality commitment is weaker than its documented performance
lessons.action: cite the performance record and request a firmer commitment as part of a package offer
lessons.why: a verified record can make a stronger commitment credible even when the supplier resists a price cut
lessons.evidence: The supplier wrote, “We checked the quality record data you cited; it holds,” and then offered the buyer's requested quality commitment.

lessons.when: a supplier prefers fewer complaint chargebacks in exchange for a lower price
lessons.action: treat waived chargebacks as a concession and weigh the price reduction against the protection lost
lessons.why: the supplier may accept the quality commitment while shifting complaint costs back to the buyer; savings are not measured by unit price alone
lessons.evidence: The buyer proposed “no per-complaint chargebacks in exchange for a lower price,” but the supplier replied that it could take that option only if “the price needs to be” higher than the buyer offered.

lessons.when: a supplier verifies a cost-index change but says that index has little effect on its costs
lessons.action: do not rely on that index alone to justify a further price cut; look for evidence tied to the supplier's main cost drivers
lessons.why: a valid index movement has limited negotiating force if it represents little of the supplier's cost base
lessons.evidence: The supplier wrote, “we checked the energy index data you cited; it holds, but it barely affects our actual costs,” and identified other main cost drivers.

lessons.when: a supplier repeatedly identifies a trade it values, but the buyer cannot offer it
lessons.action: recognise that repeating the same price request may have diminishing returns; seek another authorised trade or evaluate the standing offer
lessons.why: the supplier may tie further price movement to the unavailable trade rather than to additional argument
lessons.evidence: The supplier said, “Faster payment would help us more than anything,” then, “Since you can't offer faster payment, we really can't drop the price anymore.” Its back-office note recorded: “My call: final_offer.”

lessons.when: the supplier will hold its opening price fixed but says a longer agreement requires an index clause
lessons.action: Keep a shorter fixed-price agreement in play alongside any longer indexed offer, and compare their total value before choosing.
lessons.why: A longer commitment can change the supplier’s risk requirements. A lower base price may not compensate for the added index risk.
lessons.evidence: Opening offer: “no Preisgleitklausel.” Later: “for a contract of this duration, we cannot offer a fixed price.”

lessons.when: the supplier accepts protection against cost movements but does not lower its base price
lessons.action: Do not treat agreement on an index clause as a price concession; negotiate the base price and the clause’s risk limits together.
lessons.why: The clause protects the supplier from future increases, while the buyer still pays the agreed base price. In this deal, index risk remained after acceptance.
lessons.evidence: “With this index clause securing the material risk, we can offer a revised base price”; the buyer’s result records “index_risk” among the costs left in the deal.

lessons.when: the supplier holds its offer unchanged after receiving several buyer packages
lessons.action: Change the basis of the negotiation—such as the agreement length or allocation of cost risk—rather than repeating packages and then accepting the unchanged offer without a final trade-off.
lessons.why: Here, repeating offers did not prompt another concession: the supplier recorded successive decisions to hold, and the buyer accepted its final terms.
lessons.evidence: Back-office notes: “My call: hold.” “My call: hold.” Supplier e-mail: “This is our final offer (letztes Angebot). Please decide.”

lessons.when: the supplier cites cost indices but rejects the buyer’s analysis of those same indices
lessons.action: Ask how the claimed cost movements translate into the proposed base price, and distinguish that question from how future movements will be shared.
lessons.why: Public indices alone did not persuade this supplier to reduce its base price; it treated its underlying cost structure and future material risk as separate reasons to hold firm.
lessons.evidence: “the public indices you referenced do not alter our underlying cost structure”; “we must maintain our price.”
